column1: year|calendar,seasons|Is this photo old?~Yes. It is from last year.~Were you at school then?~Yes. I was in a different class.|The photo is from 2025. You are looking at it in 2026. Complete: It is from last ___.|year

plan|calendar,itinerary|What is our plan for Saturday?~We can visit the park.~And if it rains?~We can go to the library.|Suggest a plan for Saturday and one alternative if it rains.|We can visit the park. If it rains, we can go to the library.

goal|notebook,calendar|Are you going to read the whole book today?~No. My goal is ten pages.~Why only ten?~I can do that every day.|Make this goal easier to keep: I will read five books every week.|I will read ten pages every day.

remember|book,family|Do you remember this story?~Yes. You read it to me when I was little.~Would you like to read it now?~Yes. I remember the funny ending.|Your friend cannot recall where you met. Give one helpful detail using remember.|Do you remember the cafe near the station?

habit|tea,morning|You bring your own cup every morning.~Yes. It is a habit now.~Do you ever forget it?~Only when I leave in a hurry.|Which is a habit: buying tea once, or bringing a cup every morning? Explain.|Bringing a cup every morning is a habit because it happens regularly.

progress|growth,notebook|These drawings look different from your first ones.~I can see my progress now.~What has improved?~The shapes are clearer, and I need less time.|Name one visible sign of progress in learning to draw.|The shapes are clearer than before.

priority|checklist,calendar|Can we add another activity?~Not yet. Finishing the entrance signs is our priority.~Why start there?~Visitors need to find us before they can join anything.|Two tasks remain: a decorative poster and an essential entrance sign. State your priority and reason.|The entrance sign is my priority because visitors need to find the event.

realistic|calendar,budget|Could we finish all six rooms tonight?~Two rooms would be more realistic.~Then what happens to the others?~We can schedule them for next week.|Make this promise realistic: We will repaint six rooms in one evening with two volunteers.|We will repaint two rooms tonight and arrange another session for the rest.

retrospective|notebook,seasons|Are these notes for next month's plan?~They are a retrospective account of what we actually did.~Including the things that failed?~Especially those. Otherwise we learn very little.|Does a retrospective review primarily examine past events or predict future ones? Explain.|It examines past events so that people can understand and learn from them.

sustainable|recycling,plant|We managed an hour every evening this week.~But is that pace sustainable once work gets busy?~Probably not. Twenty minutes would be easier to maintain.~Then let us build the routine around that.|A learner studies three hours daily, becomes exhausted and stops. Propose a more sustainable arrangement.|A shorter regular session with time to rest would be easier to maintain.

teleology|growth,strategy|Does the account explain how the organization changed?~It presents every change as a step toward its current success.~So the outcome seems to explain the whole history?~Yes. That teleology leaves failed and abandoned possibilities out of view.|A history treats the present outcome as the inevitable purpose of every earlier event. Identify the limitation of this teleology.|It reads an apparent end purpose back into events and can conceal contingency and unrealized alternatives.

reflexivity|notebook,discussion|Did your role as interviewer affect the answers?~That is why I included a section on reflexivity.~What did you examine?~How my questions and institutional position shaped what people felt able to say.|Add one reflexive question to a researcher's field notes.|How might my position or assumptions have influenced the responses I recorded?
plate|meal,portion|Where can I put the bread?~On this plate.~Is this one for the soup?~No. Use the bowl for soup.|Choose plate or cup: Put the sandwich on a ___.|plate
cup|tea,water|Is this your cup?~Yes. My tea is in it.~Can I use the blue one?~Of course. It is clean.|Offer your visitor a cup of tea in one short question.|Would you like a cup of tea?

guest|serving,meal|Is Mia eating with us?~Yes. She is our guest today.~Shall I get another chair?~Yes, and a plate, please.|There are four family members and one invited guest. How many places are needed?|Five places.

prepare|serving,produce|Can I help you prepare lunch?~Please wash the carrots.~Should I cut them too?~Yes, but wash them first.|Put these actions in order: cut the carrots; wash the carrots; serve the soup.|Wash the carrots, cut them, then serve the soup.

portion|portion,meal|Would you like a larger portion?~A small one, please. I have already eaten.~You can have more later.~Thank you. That will help avoid waste.|A guest wants less food than the others. Offer an appropriate portion without commenting on their appetite.|Would you prefer a smaller portion? You can always have more later.

considerate|listening,serving|You saved the quiet seat for Daniel.~Yes. He said conversation is easier away from the speaker.~That was considerate of you.~It was a small change, but it made a difference.|A guest asks for a quieter seat. Name a considerate response.|Offer a seat away from the speaker and check whether it suits them.

hospitality|serving,meal|I was worried about arriving so late.~You were still welcome. Hospitality does not end at eight.~Even after everyone had eaten?~We kept a plate for you and made some tea.|Which demonstrates hospitality more clearly: an expensive room or making a late guest feel welcome? Explain.|Welcoming the late guest shows friendly and generous treatment, regardless of the room's price.

accommodate|room,chair|Can the room accommodate twenty people?~Seated comfortably, no. We should use the larger space.~Could we move the tables?~That would help, but we still need clear access.|The room seats twelve and sixteen guests are coming. Suggest how to accommodate everyone comfortably.|Move the gathering to a larger room or arrange another suitable seating area.

convivial|sharing,meal|Did the dinner feel formal?~Not at all. It was a wonderfully convivial evening.~What made it work?~People passed dishes around and stayed talking long after dessert.|Describe a convivial meal without using the word friendly.|Everyone shared dishes, laughed together and lingered over conversation.

reciprocity|sharing,helping|Do we owe them exactly the same favor?~Reciprocity need not mean keeping an exact account.~How might we respond, then?~Offer help when they need it, rather than calculating an equal return.|Distinguish reciprocity from a commercial exchange with a fixed price.|Reciprocity involves responding to another's help or generosity; the return need not be immediate or exactly equal.

commensality|meal,sharing|The project records more than what families eat.~Does it also examine who shares the table?~Yes. Commensality is central to the study.~Then seating, invitation and exclusion matter as much as the menu.|Why might a study of commensality record who is invited to eat, rather than only the ingredients?|Eating together is a social practice shaped by relationships, participation and exclusion.

solicitude|listening,family|She noticed he had stopped joining the conversation.~Did she ask what was wrong?~Quietly, with solicitude rather than public concern.~That gave him room to answer without becoming the center of attention.|Rewrite We all demanded to know what was wrong to convey solicitude and respect for privacy.|One person quietly asked whether he needed anything and gave him room to respond.
train|station,train|Is that our train?~No. Ours comes at ten.~Where do we wait?~On platform two.|Ask which platform your train leaves from.|Which platform does our train leave from?

ticket|ticket,ticket-gate|Do you have your ticket?~Yes. It is on my phone.~Does the gate read it?~Yes. Hold the code here.|Your phone battery is low. Suggest one way to keep your ticket available.|Save a printed copy or keep a charged device available.

journey|train,map|Was the journey tiring?~A little, but the view from the train was lovely.~Did you need to change trains?~Only once, at the coast.|Describe a journey with one transport detail and one personal impression.|We changed trains at the coast, and I enjoyed the sea view.

arrive|station,clock|What time do we arrive?~At half past six.~Will the cafe still be open?~Yes. It closes at seven.|You arrive at 6:30 and the cafe closes at 7:00. How much time is left?|Thirty minutes.

connection|station,ticket|Our first train is running late.~Will we miss the connection?~There are twenty minutes between trains, so we may still make it.~Let us check the next departure as well.|A connection leaves five minutes after your delayed train arrives on a distant platform. What should you check?|Check the transfer time and the next available service rather than assuming the connection is possible.

destination|map,itinerary|We have the tickets, but have you chosen the destination?~I thought you had.~I only chose a departure time.~Then we should decide where we actually want to go.|A traveler knows when to leave but not where to go. Which missing piece is the destination?|The place the traveler intends to reach.

itinerary|itinerary,map|Your itinerary has three museums before lunch.~It does look crowded when you say it aloud.~Which visit matters most?~The first one. I will leave the afternoon open.|Remove one avoidable pressure from an itinerary with three museums before lunch.|Keep the main museum visit and leave the others optional or move them to another day.

flexible|calendar,map|Must we follow the route exactly?~No. The plan is flexible if the weather changes.~Could we stop at the gardens instead?~Certainly, provided we can still catch the last train.|Explain one way a travel plan can be flexible without becoming completely unplanned.|Keep the return train fixed while allowing a choice of afternoon activities.

contingency|map,storm|What is our contingency if the ferry is cancelled?~We can take the coastal bus.~Have you checked the timetable?~Yes. The last one leaves at six.|A ferry may be cancelled. Name the information a useful contingency plan should include.|An alternative route, its departure times and any booking or access requirements.

navigate|map,itinerary|Can you navigate while I watch for the street signs?~Yes. The next turn is after the bridge.~The map shows two paths there.~Take the one that follows the river.|Explain how a map and street signs can help someone navigate together.|The map provides the route, while the signs help confirm the traveler's actual position.

serendipity|walk,city|Was that tiny gallery on your itinerary?~No. We found it while looking for somewhere to shelter.~And it became the highlight of the trip?~A small piece of serendipity, made possible by taking the wrong street.|Why is an unexpectedly delightful gallery discovery serendipity rather than simply a mistake?|The unplanned event produced a fortunate and welcome discovery.

circumspect|document,map|You sound reluctant to book it.~Circumspect, rather than opposed. The cancellation terms are unclear.~Would a written explanation resolve that?~It would give us firmer grounds for deciding.|Distinguish a circumspect response from rejecting an offer without examining it.|A circumspect person checks uncertain conditions and possible consequences before deciding.
chair|chair,room|Can I sit on this chair?~Yes. It is free.~Shall I move it near the table?~Please do.|Ask politely whether a chair is free.|Is this chair free?

window|window,room|Can you open the window?~A little. The room is warm.~Is the noise outside too loud?~No. This is fine.|The room is warm. Ask someone to open the window a little.|Could you open the window a little, please?

tidy|minimal,clothes|Your desk looks tidy.~I put the papers in a folder.~Can you still find everything?~Yes. That was the idea.|Make a desk tidy without throwing away important papers. Suggest one action.|Put the papers in a labeled folder.

shelf|library,dictionary|Where should these books go?~On the top shelf.~Can you reach it?~No. Please put them there for me.|You cannot reach a high shelf. Ask for help.|Could you put these books on the top shelf for me?

practical|repair,chair|That chair looks beautiful, but is it practical for the kitchen?~The fabric would be difficult to clean.~Then perhaps we should choose another one.~Something washable would suit us better.|A beautiful chair has fabric that stains easily. Explain why it may not be practical in a busy kitchen.|It would be difficult to clean after everyday spills.

familiar|room,walk|This room feels familiar.~We met here last spring.~That explains why I recognized the window.~The furniture has changed since then.|Complete the idea: A familiar place is one you have ___.|seen or experienced before

functional|minimal,chair|The entrance is attractive, but is it functional?~Not while that table blocks the doorway.~We could move it against the wall.~Then people could enter without squeezing past it.|Improve the function of an entrance where a table blocks the doorway.|Move the table so people can pass comfortably.

atmosphere|room,tea|The cafe has a calmer atmosphere this evening.~They have lowered the music and turned on the table lamps.~It makes conversation easier.~I would stay longer when it feels like this.|Name two details that can change a cafe's atmosphere.|The music volume and the lighting.

coherent|strategy,room|Each sign looks good on its own.~But do they form a coherent system?~Not yet. The arrows and colors follow different rules.~Let us choose one rule that visitors can recognize.|Explain why individually attractive signs may still fail to form a coherent system.|Their colors, arrows or terminology may contradict one another rather than work together.

adaptable|chair,room|Will this room still work for a workshop?~The furniture is adaptable; the tables fold and the seats move easily.~So we can change the layout?~Yes, without rebuilding the room.|Name one feature that makes a room adaptable for different activities.|Movable seating allows the layout to change.

vernacular|city,walk|Why keep the old shopfronts in the design study?~They show the neighborhood's architectural vernacular.~Even the ordinary ones?~Especially those. They reveal the local building habits rather than a single celebrated monument.|How might an ordinary shopfront illustrate a place's architectural vernacular?|It can show materials, forms and building habits characteristic of the locality.

patina|leather,repair|Would polishing away every mark improve the bag?~Not necessarily. Its patina records years of use.~Then age is not simply damage?~Exactly. We should distinguish a valued surface change from a structural fault.|A leather bag has a darkened surface and a broken strap. Which is more likely to be patina, and why?|The darkened surface may be patina developed through use; the broken strap is damage.

book|book,reading|Is this your book?~No. It is from the library.~Can I read it after you?~Yes, before I take it back.|Explain why you need to return a library book.|It belongs to the library, and someone else may want to borrow it.

page|book,notebook|Which page are we on?~Page twelve.~I have a picture on that page.~Then we have different books.|You and a friend are using different editions. What else could help locate the same passage besides the page number?|The chapter title or the opening words of the passage.

chapter|book,reading|Did you finish the book?~Only the first chapter.~Does it tell us who the traveler is?~Not yet. That is why I want to keep reading.|You have read one chapter. Does that necessarily mean you finished the book? Explain.|No. A chapter is one section of a book.

borrow|library,book|Can I borrow your book for the weekend?~Yes, if you bring it back on Monday.~May I write notes in it?~Please use a separate sheet.|Make a borrowing request that includes when you will return the item.|Could I borrow your book? I will return it on Monday.

passage|book,reading|Which passage should we discuss?~The paragraph where the narrator returns home.~The description of the empty kitchen?~Yes. It changes how we understand the visit.|Distinguish a passage in a book from a whole chapter.|A passage is a selected section of text; it need not include the whole chapter.

reflect|notebook,relaxing|You closed the book without starting the next chapter.~I wanted to reflect on the ending.~Did it change your mind about the character?~It made me less certain about my first judgment.|Give a reflective response to an ending that challenged your first impression of a character.|I first thought she was selfish, but the ending made me reconsider what she knew at the time.

interpretation|reading,book|We read the same ending differently.~Your interpretation makes the farewell hopeful.~And yours makes it final.~We should compare the details supporting each reading.|Two readers disagree about an ending. What should they compare to assess their interpretations?|The language and details that support each reading.

perspective|discussion,reading|The story changes when the sister starts narrating.~We finally see the argument from her perspective.~Does that excuse what she did?~Not automatically, but it changes what we know.|Does understanding another person's perspective require agreeing with them? Explain.|No. Understanding a viewpoint can clarify an action without endorsing it.

implicit|document,reading|The invitation never says we must bring food.~But that expectation seems implicit in the list of dishes.~We should check rather than assume.~I will ask the host directly.|An invitation lists guests beside dishes but gives no direct instruction. Identify the possible implicit expectation.|Guests may be expected to bring the dish beside their name, but the expectation should be checked.

discern|book,document|Can you discern a change in the narrator's tone?~The last paragraph is much less confident.~Which words give that impression?~The repeated perhaps and the unanswered questions.|Name two textual clues that could help someone discern uncertainty.|Hedging words such as perhaps and questions left unanswered.

polysemy|dictionary,book|The word head appears in three different contexts here.~A body part, a leader and the top of a table.~Are we looking at unrelated words?~These related senses illustrate polysemy, though their boundaries need careful analysis.|Does head meaning a body part and head meaning a leader illustrate one identical sense? Explain.|No. They are related but distinct senses, illustrating polysemy.

hermeneutic|reading,library|Why does the essay return to its opening after discussing the details?~Its hermeneutic approach treats the whole and the parts as mutually illuminating.~So interpretation is revised as the reading develops?~Yes, rather than fixed before the evidence is examined.|Describe a hermeneutic process without treating the first interpretation as final.|Read individual details in relation to the whole, then revise the account of the whole as those details become clearer.

friend|sharing,family|Is Leo your brother?~No. He is my friend.~Do you meet often?~We walk together on Sundays.|Introduce a friend and mention one activity you share.|This is my friend Leo. We walk together on Sundays.

listen|listening,headphones|Can you listen for a minute?~Yes. What happened?~I need to tell you about today.~I am listening. Take your time.|Your friend wants to talk. Write a short response showing you are ready to listen.|I am listening. Take your time.

explain|whiteboard,strategy|Can you explain this part?~The blue line shows where we start.~And the red one?~That is the way back.|Ask for an explanation of one specific part of a map.|Could you explain what the red line shows?
question|listening,discussion|Can I ask a question?~Of course.~Does everyone need a ticket?~Only the adults do.|Ask one clear question about admission to an event.|Do children need a ticket?

clarify|document,strategy|Could you clarify what you mean by early?~I mean before eight, not before the usual opening time.~That is helpful. I had understood it differently.~I will add the exact time to the message.|Replace Please arrive early with a clearer instruction that removes the ambiguity.|Please arrive before eight o'clock.

patient|listening,puzzle|This is taking longer than I expected.~Be patient with her. It is her first attempt.~Shall I show her the answer?~Ask whether she wants a hint first.|A beginner is taking time with a puzzle. Suggest a patient response.|Give them time and ask whether they would like a hint.

assumption|document,map|Why did we reserve a place for ten?~We worked on the assumption that everyone would attend.~Has anybody actually confirmed?~Only six people. We should check the others.|Identify the assumption in reserving ten seats before hearing from four invitees.|That all ten invitees will attend.

acknowledge|discussion,listening|Do I have to agree with every criticism?~No, but you can acknowledge the concern.~How would you put it?~I understand why the late change caused problems, even though I had limited options.|Acknowledge a complaint about a late change without claiming that every criticism is correct.|I understand that the late change disrupted your plans.

nuance|book,discussion|You described her answer as a refusal.~There was more nuance than that. She questioned the timing, not the idea.~Then my summary was too blunt.~Yes. Keep that distinction in the report.|A speaker supports a project but questions its timing. Rewrite She rejected the project to preserve the nuance.|She supported the project but questioned whether it should begin now.

receptive|listening,strategy|Will the team be receptive to another proposal?~They asked for alternatives, so this is a good moment.~Should I present it as a finished answer?~Better as an option they can question and improve.|How can someone be receptive to a proposal without accepting it immediately?|They can listen, ask questions and consider its merits before deciding.

intersubjective|discussion,sharing|Does the agreement exist independently of the participants?~Its meaning is intersubjective: it depends on a shared understanding.~Then a signature alone does not settle every interpretation?~No. We also need to examine how the participants understand the commitment.|Explain why a shared convention can be intersubjective without being merely one person's private opinion.|It is sustained through understandings shared and negotiated among people.

equivocation|document,discussion|The proposal says the service is free, but later mentions compulsory charges.~Is free being used in two different senses?~That is the equivocation we need to identify.~Then the revised wording should state exactly which part costs nothing.|A speaker shifts between free of charge and freely available as if they were identical. Identify the problem.|The equivocation changes the sense of free within the argument.
shop|shopping,market|Is the shop open?~Yes, until six.~Can we buy bread there?~Yes. It is near the door.|Ask whether a shop sells bread.|Do you sell bread here?

bag|bag,shopping|Do you need a bag?~No, thank you. I have one.~Is it big enough?~Yes. I am only buying two things.|Decline a shopping bag politely because you brought your own.|No, thank you. I have my own bag.

price|budget,shopping|What is the price of this one?~Twelve dollars.~And the smaller one?~Eight dollars.|One item costs twelve dollars and another eight. State the difference in price.|The difference is four dollars.

fresh|produce,market|Are these carrots fresh?~Yes. They arrived this morning.~I will take three, please.~Would you like the leaves left on?|Ask a market seller when the vegetables arrived.|When did these vegetables arrive?

compare|shopping,budget|These bags look almost the same.~Let us compare the straps and the material.~This one is cheaper.~But the other feels stronger.|Before choosing the cheaper bag, name two features worth comparing.|The strength of the material and the quality of the straps.

budget|saving,budget|Can we buy both lamps?~Not within our budget.~Then which one do we need most?~The desk lamp. The other can wait.|You can afford one lamp. Explain a choice that stays within your budget.|I will buy the desk lamp because I need it for work and postpone the decorative one.

value|repair,shopping|This coat costs more. Is it better value?~It may be if it lasts longer and can be repaired.~So price is only part of the comparison?~Exactly. We should consider use and durability too.|Explain why the cheapest coat may not offer the best value.|It may wear out quickly, making it more expensive over repeated replacements.

durable|leather,fabric|Will this fabric stand up to everyday use?~It is durable, but the seams matter as well.~Could I look at those?~Of course. Check the inside corners.|A seller calls a bag durable. Name one detail you could examine rather than relying on the claim.|Inspect the seams and the attachment points of the straps.

provenance|document,library|Why are you checking the old library stamp?~It may tell us something about the book's provenance.~Is the seller's account enough?~It is a starting point, but a record of earlier ownership would be stronger evidence.|Which concerns provenance: a torn cover or a dated record of former owners? Explain.|The ownership record concerns the object's origin and history; the torn cover concerns condition.

discerning|market,repair|She did not choose the most expensive piece.~She is a discerning buyer; she checks how things are made.~What persuaded her?~The repairable joints and the well-finished edges.|Describe a discerning purchase without equating good judgment with a high price.|The buyer compared construction, suitability and repairability before choosing.

externality|recycling,market|The low price does not include the waste left in the neighborhood.~That cost falls on people who did not make the purchase.~An externality, then?~Yes. The private transaction does not reflect all its wider effects.|Why might litter from a purchased product be a negative externality?|Its cleanup costs can fall on people outside the transaction.

frugality|saving,repair|Why repair the coat when a new one is affordable?~Frugality is not the same as buying the cheapest replacement.~What matters to you?~Using what still works and avoiding an unnecessary purchase.|Distinguish frugality from simply choosing the lowest sticker price.|Frugality uses resources carefully and may favor repair or a durable item over repeated cheap purchases.
flower|valentine,plant|Is this flower from your garden?~Yes. I picked it this morning.~Can I put it in water?~Please do.|A cut flower is beginning to wilt. Suggest one simple action.|Put it in water.

card|valentine,notebook|Did you write the card?~Yes. I thanked her for helping me.~Will you buy a gift too?~I think the card says what I wanted to say.|Write one specific thank-you sentence for a card.|Thank you for helping me move last weekend.

invite|sharing,meal|Shall we invite our new neighbor?~Yes. Ask whether Saturday suits her.~Should I mention the food?~Tell her it is a simple lunch, so she knows what to expect.|Invite a neighbor to lunch and give a day.|Would you like to join us for lunch on Saturday?

appreciate|family,listening|Did you mind staying late?~A little, but I appreciated your message afterward.~I wanted you to know your help mattered.~Next time, let us agree on the finish time first.|Show appreciation for a specific action rather than saying only Thanks for everything.|I appreciate you staying late to help clear the room.

affection|family,valentine|The note is warm without being elaborate.~It shows affection through a familiar memory.~Rather than a grand declaration?~Yes. A small shared detail can carry more feeling.|Write a brief sentence expressing affection through a shared memory.|I still smile when I remember our rainy picnic together.

platonic|sharing,valentine|Will flowers make the message sound romantic?~They might. I want to make the platonic intention clear.~Then mention your friendship directly.~Good idea. I am thanking a friend, not proposing a date.|Rewrite I cannot wait to see you so that the intended friendship is clearer.|I am looking forward to catching up with you as a friend.

interdependence|community,pollination|Could either team finish the project alone?~No. Their interdependence is built into the work.~Then one delayed handover affects the other team?~Exactly. Their responsibilities cannot be understood in isolation.|Explain interdependence using two teams that need each other's work.|Each team's progress depends partly on what the other team provides.

lantern|lunar-lantern,lunar|Who put the lantern above the door?~My aunt did.~Does it stay there all evening?~Yes. It lights the entrance.|Describe where a lantern could help visitors find an entrance.|A lantern above the door can make the entrance easier to see.

envelope|valentine,lunar|Where is the letter?~Inside the envelope.~Have you written the address?~Yes, on the front.|You have a card to post. What two things should go on the envelope?|The recipient's address and the required postage.

reunion|family,sharing|Will everyone be at the reunion?~My cousins are coming from three cities.~When did you last meet?~Five years ago, so we will have plenty to talk about.|Explain why a family reunion differs from meeting a relative you see every day.|It brings people together again after a period apart.

luck|lunar,easter-hunt|How did you find the missing ring?~Pure luck. I looked under the last chair.~You must be relieved.~I am. Now I will keep it in a box.|Was finding a ring unexpectedly under a chair necessarily the result of skill? Explain using luck.|It may have been luck: a fortunate result that was not fully controlled.

celebrate|family,independence|Are you doing anything for your graduation?~We are going to celebrate with a small dinner.~May I bring something?~A story about our first week would be lovely.|Suggest a way to celebrate an achievement without buying a large gift.|Share a meal and tell a story about the person's effort.

prosperity|market,lunar|The greeting wishes the family prosperity.~Does that refer only to having more money?~It often concerns material success and well-being.~Then the context matters when we explain it.|Paraphrase a wish for prosperity without promising that wealth is guaranteed.|May the coming year bring well-being and the conditions for a flourishing life.

auspicious|lunar-lantern,lunar|Why did they choose that date?~They regard it as auspicious.~Does everyone in the family agree?~No. We should describe it as their belief, not as a guaranteed outcome.|A family regards a date as auspicious. Does that prove the event will succeed? Explain.|No. It means the date is regarded as favorable, not that success is certain.

symbolism|lunar,ornament|Why do these objects appear in the display?~The guide explains their symbolism.~So they are doing more than decorating the room?~Yes. They can represent wishes, beliefs or remembered events.|Explain how a decorative object can also have symbolism.|It can stand for a wish, belief or memory in addition to looking attractive.

intergenerational|family,community|Who is taking part in the workshop?~Grandparents, parents and teenagers. It is deliberately intergenerational.~Will the older people do all the teaching?~No. Each group has something to contribute.|Why would an intergenerational workshop benefit from letting young people teach as well as learn?|Knowledge can move between generations in more than one direction.

continuity|seasons,family|The recipe has changed a little.~Does that break its continuity with earlier family practice?~Not necessarily. Some methods and meanings remain.~Then continuity does not require every detail to stay identical.|Can a family tradition show continuity while changing some ingredients? Explain.|Yes, if recognizable practices or meanings continue across the changes.

diaspora|family,city|The exhibition follows families across several countries.~Does it treat the diaspora as a single, uniform community?~No. It records different relationships with places of origin.~That seems essential to understanding the variety of their experiences.|Why should an account of a diaspora avoid assuming that every member has the same experience?|Dispersed communities contain different histories, identities and relationships to places of origin.

syncretism|ornament,lunar|The ceremony combines practices from different traditions.~Is that simple copying?~The historian describes a more complex process of syncretism.~Then we should examine how the elements acquire new meanings together.|Distinguish syncretism from merely placing two unrelated objects side by side.|Syncretism involves a blending or integration of traditions or beliefs, not just their proximity.
song|music,guitar|Do you know this song?~Yes. My sister sings it.~Can you sing it with me?~I know the first part.|Invite someone to sing a song with you.|Would you like to sing this song with me?

hear|headphones,music|Can you hear the guitar?~Yes, but it is very quiet.~Shall I turn it up?~Just a little, please.|Ask someone to raise the volume slightly because you cannot hear clearly.|Could you turn it up a little, please?

rhythm|guitar,music|Why are you tapping the table?~I am following the rhythm.~Can I join in?~Yes. Listen to the pattern first.|Explain rhythm without naming a particular song.|It is a pattern of beats or sounds over time.

quiet|relaxing,room|Is this a quiet place to read?~Usually, but the building work starts at nine.~Then I will come earlier.~The back room is quiet in the afternoon too.|A room is quiet until building work begins at nine. Suggest a suitable reading time.|Read there before nine or use the back room in the afternoon.

melody|guitar,music|I recognize the melody, but not these words.~It is a different version of the same song.~That explains why I could hum it.~The tune stayed familiar even when the lyrics changed.|A song's words change but its tune remains. Which part is the melody?|The tune.

attention|headphones,listening|Did you notice the change in the final verse?~No. My attention was on the message I was typing.~Shall we listen again without our phones?~Yes.
